claim: Multisensory information offers substantial benefits for behavior, such as combining acoustic and visual cues to derive a more reliable estimate of object location.
source: Multisensory information offers substantial benefits for behavior. For example, acoustic and visual cues can be combined to derive a more reliable estimate of where an object is located (Alais and Burr, 2004; Ernst and Banks, 2002; Körding et al., 2007; Wozny and Shams, 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research demonstrating this phenomenon.

claim: Multisensory information can be exploited to calibrate subsequent perception in the absence of external feedback.
source: Yet, the process of multisensory perception does not end once an object is removed. In fact, multisensory information can be exploited to calibrate subsequent perception in the absence of external feedback (Frissen et al., 2012; Wozny and Shams, 2011a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In a ventriloquist paradigm, both visual and auditory cues influence the localization of subsequent unisensory acoustic cues.
source: In a ventriloquist paradigm, for example, the sight of the puppet and the actor's voice are combined when localizing the speech source, and both cues influence the localization of subsequent unisensory acoustic cues, if probed experimentally (Bosen et al., 2017; Bosen et al., 2018; Bruns and Röder, 2015; Bruns and Röder, 2017; Callan et al., 2015; Radeau and Bertelson, 1974; Recanzone, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental research.

claim: Trial-by-trial recalibration of perception by previous multisensory information has been demonstrated for spatial cues, temporal cues, and speech signals.
source: This trial-by-trial recalibration of perception by previous multisensory information has been demonstrated for spatial cues, temporal cues, and speech signals (Kilian-Hütten et al., 2011a; Lüttke et al., 2016; Lüttke et al., 2018; Van der Burg et al., 2013), and has been shown to be modulated by attention (Eramudugolla et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research demonstrating these effects.

claim: It remains unclear whether multisensory integration and trial-by-trial recalibration originate from shared neural mechanisms.
source: Despite the importance of both facets of multisensory perception for adaptive behavior - the combination of information within a trial and the trial-by-trial adjustment of perception - it remains unclear whether they originate from shared neural mechanisms.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge, which is the motivation for the study.

claim: The neural underpinnings of trial-by-trial recalibration remain largely unclear.
source: In fact, the neural underpinnings of trial-by-trial recalibration remain largely unclear.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Studies on neural correlates of multisensory recalibration mostly focused on adaptation following long-term exposure to consistent multisensory discrepancies.
source: Those studies that have investigated neural correlates of multisensory recalibration mostly focused on the adaptation following long-term (that is, often minutes of) exposure to consistent multisensory discrepancies (Bruns et al., 2011; Zierul et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Recalibration after a few exposure trials is best explained in head coordinates.
source: However, this study also noted that a transition from head- to mixed-spatial representations emerges slowly and only after prolonged exposure, while recalibration after a few exposure trials is best explained in head coordinates.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: The neural underpinnings of multisensory integration of simultaneously received information have been investigated in many paradigms and model systems.
source: In contrast to this, the neural underpinnings of multisensory integration of simultaneously received information have been investigated in many paradigms and model systems (Angelaki et al., 2009; Bizley et al., 2016; Fetsch et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Studies on spatial ventriloquist-like paradigms demonstrate contributions from auditory and parietal cortex.
source: Studies on spatial ventriloquist-like paradigms, for example, demonstrate contributions from auditory and parietal cortex (Bonath et al., 2014; Bruns and Röder, 2010; Bruns and Röder, 2015; Callan et al., 2015; Harvey et al., 2014; Bonath et al., 2007; Starke et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Posterior parietal regions automatically fuse multisensory information, while anterior parietal regions give way to a more flexible spatial representation that follows predictions from Bayesian causal inference.
source: A series of recent studies demonstrates that posterior parietal regions automatically fuse multisensory information, while anterior parietal regions give way to a more flexible spatial representation that follows predictions from Bayesian causal inference (Cao et al., 2019; Rohe et al., 2019; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015b; Rohe and Noppeney, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: Parietal regions contribute to the maintenance of sensory information within or between trials.
source: Given that parietal regions also contribute to the maintenance of sensory information within or between trials (Harvey et al., 2012; Morcos and Harvey, 2016; Raposo et al., 2014; Schott et al., 2018; Uncapher and Wagner, 2009; Vilberg and Rugg, 2008) this raises the possibility that parietal regions are in fact mediating both the combination of sensory information within a trial, and the influence of such an integrated representation on guiding subsequent adaptive behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: 24 volunteering participants participated in the study.
source: Twenty-six healthy right-handed adults participated in this study (15 females, age 24.2 ± 4.7 years).
evidence: The claim is based on the reported participant count after exclusions.

claim: Data from two participants had to be excluded due to technical problems during acquisition.
source: Data from two participants (both females) had to be excluded as these were incomplete due to technical problems during acquisition, hence results are reported for 24 participants.
evidence: The claim is based on the reported exclusion criteria.

claim: Behavioral responses in AV trials revealed a clear ventriloquist effect as a function of the presented audio-visual discrepancy.
source: Behavioral responses in AV trials revealed a clear ventriloquist effect (VE) as a function of the presented audio-visual discrepancy (ΔVA = VAV  - AAV), whereby the visual stimulus biased the perceived sound location (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Model comparison revealed that both auditory and visual stimuli had a significant influence on the participants' responses in AV trials.
source: Model comparison revealed that both stimuli had a significant influence on the participants' responses (relative BIC values of three candidate models, c.f. Materials and methods Section: mi1: 938, mi2: 3816, mi3: 0; relative AIC values; mi1: 945, mi2: 3823, mi3: 0; protected exceedance probability (Rigoux et al., 2014); mi1: 0, mi2: 0, mi3: 1; winning model: mi3: VE ~ 1 + β⋅AAV + β⋅VAV), with significant contributions from both the auditory (AAV), and visual stimuli (VAV) (βA_AV = -0.48, βV_AV = 0.22, tA_AV = -70.0, tV_AV = 31.7, pA_AV, pV_AV <0.01, d.f. = 8064).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical model comparison and regression results.

claim: Across participants, the VE bias was significant for each non-zero audio-visual discrepancy.
source: Across participants, the VE bias was significant for each non-zero audio-visual discrepancy (all p<10−4; Wilcoxon signed rank tests, corrected for multiple tests with the Holm procedure).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing of the behavioral data.

claim: Behavioral responses in A trials revealed a significant ventriloquist aftereffect as a function of the audio-visual discrepancy in the previous AV trial.
source: Behavioral responses in A trials revealed a significant ventriloquist aftereffect (VAE; Figure 1D) as a function of the audio-visual discrepancy (ΔVA) in the previous AV trial, demonstrating that the preceding multisensory stimuli had a lasting influence on the localization of subsequent sounds.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Model comparison revealed that both previous auditory and visual stimuli had a significant influence on the VAE.
source: Model comparison revealed that both previous stimuli had a significant influence on the VAE (relative BIC values of three candidate models, c.f. Materials and methods section; mr1: 27, mr2: 357, mr3: 0; relative AIC values: mr1: 34, mr2: 364, mr3: 0; protected exceedance probability; mr1: 0, mr2: 0, mr3: 1; winning model: mr3: VAE ~ 1 + β⋅AAV + β⋅VAV), with significant contributions from the previous sound (AAV), and the previous visual stimulus (VAV) (βA_AV = -0.09, βV_AV = 0.03, tA_AV = -19.4, tV_AV = 6.0, pA_AV, pV_AV <0.01, d.f. = 8064).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical model comparison and regression results.

claim: Across participants, the VAE bias was significant for each non-zero audio-visual discrepancy.
source: Across participants, the VAE bias was significant for each non-zero audio-visual discrepancy (all p<10−2; two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank tests, corrected for multiple tests with the Holm procedure).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing of the behavioral data.

claim: The VAE was clearly in favor of a genuine multisensory bias rather than a bias towards the previous visual stimulus location.
source: The data were clearly in favor of a genuine multisensory bias, as the VAE remained significant for these trials (all p<0.05; except for +25.5 condition; two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank tests, corrected for multiple tests; Figure 1F) (Wozny and Shams, 2011a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing of selected trials shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The model RA ~1 + AA + ΔVA provided a better account of the data than a response-based model RA ~1 + AA + RAV.
source: Formal model comparison revealed that the model RA ~1 + AA + ΔVA provided a better account of the data than a response-based model RA ~1 + AA + RAV (relative BIC: 0, 393; BIC weights: 1, 0), supporting the notion that recalibration is linked more to the physical stimuli than the participants response (Van der Burg et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by formal model comparison using BIC.

claim: Significant classification performance for the current sound (AA) was obtained from MEG activity during the A trials, peaking at 80 ms in the left inferior parietal and at 160 ms in the middle temporal gyrus.
source: From the MEG activity during the A trials, we obtained significant classification (cluster-based permutation test, correcting for multiple comparisons, for details refer to Materials and methods - Statistical Analysis) performance for the current sound (AA; peaking at 80 ms in the left inferior parietal and at 160 ms in the middle temporal gyrus) and for the location of the sound in the previous trial (AAV; peaking around 120 ms in the left middle occipital lobe and the bilateral precuneus; at p≤0.01 FWE corrected for multiple comparisons in source space).
evidence: The claim is supported by MEG classification analysis with statistical correction.

claim: Significant classification performance for the location of the sound in the previous trial (AAV) was obtained from MEG activity during the A trials, peaking around 120 ms in the left middle occipital lobe and the bilateral precuneus.
source: From the MEG activity during the A trials, we obtained significant classification (cluster-based permutation test, correcting for multiple comparisons, for details refer to Materials and methods - Statistical Analysis) performance for the current sound (AA; peaking at 80 ms in the left inferior parietal and at 160 ms in the middle temporal gyrus) and for the location of the sound in the previous trial (AAV; peaking around 120 ms in the left middle occipital lobe and the bilateral precuneus; at p≤0.01 FWE corrected for multiple comparisons in source space).
evidence: The claim is supported by MEG classification analysis with statistical correction.

claim: Classification of the lateralization of previous visual stimuli (VAV) was not significant at the whole brain level in the activity of the A trial.
source: Classification of the lateralization of previous visual stimuli (VAV) was not significant at the whole brain level in the activity of the A trial, suggesting that persistent visual information was weaker than that of the acoustic information.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of classification analysis.

claim: The whole brain classification maps revealed meaningful clusters for VAV in early left inferior temporal areas and the right inferior/superior parietal areas.
source: However, the whole brain classification maps revealed meaningful clusters in early left inferior temporal areas and the right inferior/superior parietal areas.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of classification analysis.

claim: Classification of the upcoming response (RA) was significant with a similar pattern as observed for the current sound (AA) in the A trial.
source: Classification of the upcoming response (RA) was significant with a similar pattern as observed for the current sound (AA) in the A trial.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of classification analysis.

claim: There was a significant influence of AAV on the encoding of sound AA in the MEG activity of the A trial, starting around 80 ms in the cingulum, precuneus, shifting towards inferior/superior parietal areas around 220 ms.
source: There was a significant (cluster-based permutation test FWE corrected at p≤0.05) influence of AAV, starting around 80 ms in the cingulum, precuneus, shifting towards inferior/superior parietal areas around 220 ms.
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis of MEG data with statistical correction.

claim: There was a significant influence of VAV on the encoding of sound AA in the MEG activity of the A trial in the left occipital/parietal areas around 160 ms.
source: There was also significant influence of VAV in the left occipital/parietal areas around 160 ms.
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis of MEG data with statistical correction.

claim: The significant effects from the previous acoustic and visual stimuli overlapped in the left parietal areas.
source: Importantly, the significant effects from the previous acoustic and visual stimuli overlapped in the left parietal areas (Figure 3A; red inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both previous sound and visual stimulus influenced the activity predictive of the current response around 80 ms in the right parietal cortex (precuneus in particular).
source: In particular, both previous sound and visual stimulus influenced the activity predictive of the current response around 80 ms in the right parietal cortex (precuneus in particular), with the effect of AAV including also frontal and temporal regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis of MEG data.

claim: The significant effects of AAV and VAV on the response overlapped in the cingulum and precuneus.
source: The significant effects of AAV and VAV overlapped in the cingulum and precuneus (Figure 3B; red inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by the overlap analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Parietal regions represent information about previous multisensory stimuli, and this information affects the neural encoding of the currently perceived sound.
source: These results demonstrate that parietal regions represent information about previous multisensory stimuli, and this information affects the neural encoding of the currently perceived sound.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: The significant influences of the neural representations of previous acoustic and visual stimuli on the VAE overlapped in parietal cortex (angular gyrus, precuneus).
source: The significant influences of the neural representations of previous acoustic and visual stimuli overlapped again in parietal cortex (angular gyrus, precuneus; Figure 3C; red inset).
evidence: The claim is supported by the neuro-behavioral analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The same parietal regions retain information about both previously received acoustic and visual spatial information, and single trial variations in these neural representations directly influence the participants' bias of subsequent sound localization.
source: The converging evidence from these three analyses demonstrates that the same parietal regions retain information about both previously received acoustic and visual spatial information, and that single trial variations in these neural representations directly influence the participants' bias of subsequent sound localization.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined results from multiple analyses.

claim: Classification for both auditory (AAV) and visual (VAV) locations was significant in a network of temporal and occipital regions in the AV trial.
source: As expected from the above, classification for both auditory (AAV) and visual (VAV) locations was significant in a network of temporal and occipital regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by classification analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overlapping representations of both auditory and visual stimuli that directly correlated with the response bias within superior parietal regions (precuneus and superior parietal lobule) were revealed in the AV trial.
source: This revealed overlapping representations of both stimuli that directly correlated with the response bias within superior parietal regions (precuneus and superior parietal lobule), and, in a separate cluster, within inferior temporal areas (Figure 4; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by neuro-behavioral analysis shown in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: Overlapping representations of both auditory and visual stimuli that directly correlated with the response bias within inferior temporal areas were revealed in the AV trial.
source: This revealed overlapping representations of both stimuli that directly correlated with the response bias within superior parietal regions (precuneus and superior parietal lobule), and, in a separate cluster, within inferior temporal areas (Figure 4; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by neuro-behavioral analysis shown in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: The spatially selective activity contributing to the VE effect (CPAR) also significantly contributes to the VAE effect.
source: This revealed that the spatially selective activity contributing to the VE effect (CPAR, from Figure 4) also significantly contributes to the VAE effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-testing the neuro-behavioral models in different clusters.

claim: The effect strength in cluster CPAR for recalibration did not differ from that observed in the cluster directly identified as significantly contributing to the VAE bias (CVAE).
source: Further, the effect strength in this cluster for recalibration did not differ from that observed in the cluster directly identified as significantly contributing to the VAE bias (CVAE, at p<0.05; FDR adjusted; Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of effect sizes between clusters.

claim: The parietal sources mediating recalibration (cluster CVAE) also significantly contributed to sensory integration within the AV trial.
source: Vice versa, we found that the parietal sources mediating recalibration (cluster CVAE; from Figure 3C) also significantly contributed to sensory integration within the AV trial (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-testing the neuro-behavioral models in different clusters.

claim: Spatially selective activity within superior parietal regions (identified by both clusters, CPAR, and CVAE, comprising precuneus and superior parietal regions) is significantly contributing to both sensory integration and trial-by-trial recalibration.
source: These results confirm that spatially selective activity within superior parietal regions (identified by both clusters, CPAR, and CVAE, comprising precuneus and superior parietal regions) is significantly contributing to both sensory integration and trial-by-trial recalibration.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the cross-testing results.

claim: The overall evidence for the neural correlates of the VE bias to be lateralized was weak, and absent for the parietal contribution.
source: Hence, the overall evidence for the neural correlates of the VE bias to be lateralized was weak, and absent for the parietal contribution.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical testing of hemispheric differences.

claim: For parietal activity in the AV trial (clusters CVAE and CPAR) discriminant performance was significantly higher for the weighted multisensory than for unisensory AAV information.
source: For parietal activity in the AV trial (clusters CVAE and CPAR) discriminant performance was significantly higher for the weighted multisensory than for unisensory AAV information (two-sided paired t-test, p≤3*10−6, for both comparisons, FDR corrected; Figure 5), confirming that these regions indeed encode the integrated multisensory information.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of classification performance shown in Figure 5.

claim: Parietal regions encode the integrated multisensory information.
source: For parietal activity in the AV trial (clusters CVAE and CPAR) discriminant performance was significantly higher for the weighted multisensory than for unisensory AAV information (two-sided paired t-test, p≤3*10−6, for both comparisons, FDR corrected; Figure 5), confirming that these regions indeed encode the integrated multisensory information.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the classification performance comparison.

claim: Temporal activity (CTEMP) was equally sensitive to unisensory and combined multisensory information in both trials.
source: In contrast, temporal activity (CTEMP) was equally sensitive to unisensory and combined multisensory information in both trials, in line with temporal regions participating both in sensory integration and unisensory processing (Beauchamp et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by classification performance comparison and citation to prior research.

claim: Only 4.9 ± 1.7% (mean ± s.e.m) of trials exhibited evidence of potential eye-movements across all participants.
source: This revealed that only 4.9 ± 1.7% (mean ± s.e.m) of trials exhibited evidence of potential eye-movements across all participants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ICA components reflecting eye movements.

claim: Eye-movements during the stimulus presentation period were rare (0.35 ± 0.12%, max 2.2%).
source: In particular, eye-movements during the stimulus presentation period were rare (0.35 ± 0.12%, max 2.2%).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of ICA components reflecting eye movements.

claim: Superior medial parietal activity represents current auditory and visual information, encodes the combined multisensory estimate as reflected in participant's behavior, and retains information during the subsequent trial.
source: Using single trial MEG analysis we determined a network of temporal and parietal brain regions that mediate behavioral sound localization. Of these regions, superior medial parietal activity represents current auditory and visual information, encodes the combined multisensory estimate as reflected in participant's behavior, and retains information during the subsequent trial.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings from the MEG analysis.

claim: Parietal representations mediate both the multisensory integration within a trial and the subsequent recalibration of unisensory auditory perception.
source: Importantly, these parietal representations mediate both the multisensory integration within a trial and the subsequent recalibration of unisensory auditory perception, suggesting a common neural substrate for sensory integration and trial-by-trial recalibration of subsequent unisensory perception.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined results from the neuro-behavioral analyses.

claim: There is a common neural substrate for sensory integration and trial-by-trial recalibration of subsequent unisensory perception.
source: Importantly, these parietal representations mediate both the multisensory integration within a trial and the subsequent recalibration of unisensory auditory perception, suggesting a common neural substrate for sensory integration and trial-by-trial recalibration of subsequent unisensory perception.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the combined results from the neuro-behavioral analyses.

claim: Persistent representations of previous acoustic information were found in a temporal-parietal network.
source: This revealed persistent representations of previous acoustic information in a temporal-parietal network, suggesting that the regions known to reflect auditory spatial information within a trial also retain previous sensory evidence to mediate behavior (At et al., 2011; Bizley and Cohen, 2013; Lewald et al., 2008; Zimmer and Macaluso, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by the classification analysis and citations to prior research.

claim: The regions known to reflect auditory spatial information within a trial also retain previous sensory evidence to mediate behavior.
source: This revealed persistent representations of previous acoustic information in a temporal-parietal network, suggesting that the regions known to reflect auditory spatial information within a trial also retain previous sensory evidence to mediate behavior (At et al., 2011; Bizley and Cohen, 2013; Lewald et al., 2008; Zimmer and Macaluso, 2005).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the classification results supported by citations.

claim: The perceptual bias induced by vision on sound localization (i.e. the ventriloquist effect) is mediated by the posterior middle temporal gyrus and the superior parietal cortex.
source: Our results suggest that the perceptual bias induced by vision on sound localization (i.e. the ventriloquist effect) is mediated by the posterior middle temporal gyrus and the superior parietal cortex, with parietal regions encoding the perceptually combined multisensory information.
evidence: The claim is based on the neuro-behavioral analysis of the VE.

claim: Parietal regions encode the perceptually combined multisensory information.
source: Our results suggest that the perceptual bias induced by vision on sound localization (i.e. the ventriloquist effect) is mediated by the posterior middle temporal gyrus and the superior parietal cortex, with parietal regions encoding the perceptually combined multisensory information.
evidence: The claim is based on the classification performance comparison for combined vs. unisensory information.

claim: Both temporal and parietal regions combine audio-visual information in a reliability- and task-dependent manner.
source: In particular, a series of studies revealed that both temporal and parietal regions combine audio-visual information in a reliability- and task-dependent manner (Aller and Noppeney, 2019; Rohe et al., 2019; Rohe and Noppeney, 2015b; Rohe and Noppeney, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Posterior parietal regions reflect the automatic fusion of multisensory information, while more anterior parietal regions reflect an adaptive multisensory representation that follows predictions of Bayesian inference models.
source: However, while posterior parietal regions reflect the automatic fusion of multisensory information, more anterior parietal regions reflect an adaptive multisensory representation that follows predictions of Bayesian inference models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Anterior parietal regions (sub-divisions IPS3 and 4) combine multisensory information when two cues seem to arise from a common origin and only partially integrate when there is a chance that the two cues arise from distinct sources.
source: These anterior regions (sub-divisions IPS3 and 4 in Rohe and Noppeney, 2015b) combine multisensory information when two cues seem to arise from a common origin and only partially integrate when there is a chance that the two cues arise from distinct sources, in accordance with the flexible use of discrepant multisensory information for behavior (Cao et al., 2019; Körding et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The results corroborate the behavioral relevance of superior-anterior parietal representations.
source: Our results hence corroborate the behavioral relevance of superior-anterior parietal representations and fit with an interpretation that these regions mediate the flexible use of multisensory information, depending on task and sensory congruency, to mediate adaptive behavior.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results in the context of prior research.

claim: Superior-anterior parietal regions mediate the flexible use of multisensory information, depending on task and sensory congruency, to mediate adaptive behavior.
source: Our results hence corroborate the behavioral relevance of superior-anterior parietal representations and fit with an interpretation that these regions mediate the flexible use of multisensory information, depending on task and sensory congruency, to mediate adaptive behavior.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results in the context of prior research.

claim: Very little is known about the brain regions implementing the trial-by-trial recalibration of unisensory perception by previous multisensory information.
source: In contrast, very little is known about the brain regions implementing the trial-by-trial recalibration of unisensory perception by previous multisensory information.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Most studies on neural correlates of multisensory recalibration have relied on prolonged adaptation to multisensory discrepancies.
source: In fact, most studies have relied on prolonged adaptation to multisensory discrepancies.
evidence: The claim characterizes the prior research literature.

claim: Long-term recalibration seems to be mechanistically distinct from the trial-by-trial recalibration investigated in this study.
source: Hence these studies investigated long-term recalibration, which seems to be mechanistically distinct from the trial-by-trial recalibration investigated here (Bosen et al., 2017; Bruns et al., 2011; Bruns and Röder, 2010; Bonath et al., 2007; Zierul et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ventriloquist after-effect is mediated by an interaction of auditory and parietal regions.
source: The study most closely resembling the present one suggested that the ventriloquist after-effect is mediated by an interaction of auditory and parietal regions (Zierul et al., 2017), a network centered view also supported by work on the McGurk after-effect (Kilian-Hütten et al., 2011a; Kilian-Hütten et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: No study to date has investigated the direct underpinnings of multisensory recalibration at the trial-by-trial level, or attempted to directly link the neural signature of the encoded sensory information about previous stimuli to the participant-specific perceptual bias.
source: Yet, no study to date has investigated the direct underpinnings of multisensory recalibration at the trial-by-trial level, or attempted to directly link the neural signature of the encoded sensory information about previous stimuli to the participant-specific perceptual bias.
evidence: The claim identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The results demonstrate the behavioral relevance of anterior medial parietal representations of previous multisensory information.
source: Our results close this gap by demonstrating the behavioral relevance of anterior medial parietal representations of previous multisensory information, which seem to reflect the flexible combination of spatial information following multisensory causal inference, and have a direct influence on participants' perceptual bias in localizing a subsequent unisensory stimulus.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the neuro-behavioral analysis results.

claim: Anterior medial parietal representations reflect the flexible combination of spatial information following multisensory causal inference.
source: Our results close this gap by demonstrating the behavioral relevance of anterior medial parietal representations of previous multisensory information, which seem to reflect the flexible combination of spatial information following multisensory causal inference, and have a direct influence on participants' perceptual bias in localizing a subsequent unisensory stimulus.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results in the context of prior research on Bayesian causal inference.

claim: Anterior medial parietal representations have a direct influence on participants' perceptual bias in localizing a subsequent unisensory stimulus.
source: Our results close this gap by demonstrating the behavioral relevance of anterior medial parietal representations of previous multisensory information, which seem to reflect the flexible combination of spatial information following multisensory causal inference, and have a direct influence on participants' perceptual bias in localizing a subsequent unisensory stimulus.
evidence: The claim is based on the neuro-behavioral analysis linking neural representations to behavioral bias.

claim: The retention of information about previous stimuli in parietal cortex directly links to animal work showing mixed patterns of neural selectivity in parietal cortex.
source: The retention of information about previous stimuli in parietal cortex directly links to animal work, which has revealed a mixed pattern of neural selectivity in parietal cortex, with individual neurons encoding both unisensory and multisensory information, reflecting the accumulation of this over time, and the transformation into perceptual choice (Raposo et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim connects the current findings to prior animal research.

claim: Parietal neurons are involved in maintaining the history of prior stimulus information.
source: For example, parietal neurons are involved in maintaining the history of prior stimulus information, a role that is directly in line with our results (Akrami et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The previously experienced stimuli shape both the neural encoding of the subsequent sound and neural correlates of the upcoming response.
source: Also, the observation that the previously experienced stimuli shape both the neural encoding of the subsequent sound and neural correlates of the upcoming response (Figure 3A,B) suggests that these representations of prior evidence emerge in a neural system intermediate between pure sensory and pure motor (or choice) representations.
evidence: The claim is based on the regression analysis results shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Representations of prior evidence emerge in a neural system intermediate between pure sensory and pure motor (or choice) representations.
source: Also, the observation that the previously experienced stimuli shape both the neural encoding of the subsequent sound and neural correlates of the upcoming response (Figure 3A,B) suggests that these representations of prior evidence emerge in a neural system intermediate between pure sensory and pure motor (or choice) representations.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the regression analysis results.

claim: The medial superior parietal cortex has been implied in maintaining spatial and episodic memory used for example during navigation, spatial updating or spatial search.
source: In humans, the medial superior parietal cortex pinpointed here as mediator of recalibration has been implied in maintaining spatial and episodic memory (Müller et al., 2018; Pollmann et al., 2003; Schott et al., 2018; Uncapher and Wagner, 2009; Vilberg and Rugg, 2008) used for example during navigation, spatial updating or spatial search (Brodt et al., 2016; Pollmann et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The results broaden the functional scope of medial parietal regions in multisensory perception, by showing that these regions are also involved in the integration of multiple simultaneous cues to guide subsequent spatial behavior.
source: Our results broaden the functional scope of these parietal regions in multisensory perception, by showing that these regions are also involved in the integration of multiple simultaneous cues to guide subsequent spatial behavior.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results in the context of prior research.

claim: The medial parietal cortex is at the interface of momentary sensory inference and memory.
source: This places the medial parietal cortex at the interface of momentary sensory inference and memory, and exposes multisensory recalibration as a form of implicit episodic memory, mediating the integration of past and current information into a more holistic percept.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the results in the context of prior research on memory.

claim: Multisensory recalibration is a form of implicit episodic memory, mediating the integration of past and current information into a more holistic percept.
